title: Inflammatory Diseases of the Reproductive Tract
subject: Reproductive System (REPR)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers inflammation of the male and female reproductive tracts and two conditions in which endometrium grows where it does not belong. It begins with local infections of the glans and cervix, covers endometriosis, adenomyosis, endometritis, and orchitis, follows infection upward from the cervix to the tubes and peritoneum, and ends with vulvovaginal disease. NPLEX Part I cases usually give the diagnosis and ask for the organism, the tissue change, the risk factor, or the complication. If you know which epithelium each organism targets, how inflammation heals by scarring, and how estrogen drives misplaced endometrium, you can predict most of the findings.
prerequisites: Histology of the female tract: squamous vagina and ectocervix, columnar endocervix, ciliated tubal mucosa
Menstrual cycle hormones and the functional and basal layers of the endometrium
Anatomy of the penis, scrotum, testis, epididymis, and vas deferens
Peritoneal spaces: rectouterine pouch and paracolic gutters
Acute and chronic inflammation, healing by fibrosis, and cell-mediated immunity

connections.to: Microbiology of sexually transmitted and opportunistic organisms
connections.how: The cell biology of Chlamydia, Neisseria, Trichomonas, HSV, and Candida explains which epithelium each infects and what it looks like.
T-cell immunity controls mucosal Candida, and the immune response to persistent Chlamydia, rather than the organism alone, scars the fallopian tube.
Estrogen maintains vaginal glycogen and acidity and drives the growth of endometriosis, adenomyosis, and leiomyoma.
Tubal scarring predisposes to ectopic pregnancy, and delivery creates the setting for acute endometritis.
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis mimics cholecystitis, and lichen sclerosus precedes HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma.

sections.title: Balanitis and its link to phimosis

blocks.text: Balanitis is inflammation of the glans penis. When the inner surface of the foreskin is also inflamed, as it usually is in uncircumcised men, the term is balanoposthitis. The preputial sac between glans and foreskin is warm and moist and collects smegma, a mixture of shed epithelial cells, glandular secretions, and urine residue. When this material is not cleared, it supports overgrowth of organisms that are normally held in check.

Candida albicans is the most common infectious cause. Bacterial causes include anaerobes, streptococci (groups A and B), Staphylococcus aureus, and Gardnerella vaginalis, sometimes acquired from a sexual partner. Noninfectious balanitis also occurs from irritants, contact dermatitis, and skin diseases such as lichen sclerosus (C10). The inflamed glans is red, swollen, sore, and itchy, sometimes with a discharge under the foreskin; candidal balanitis often shows patchy redness with small papules or a white film, while anaerobic infection tends to be malodorous.

blocks.title: Risk factors for balanitis and how each works
rows: Creates a closed, moist preputial sac where smegma and organisms collect
Smegma and urine residue are not removed from the sac
Glucose in urine residue feeds Candida, and hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil chemotaxis and killing
The foreskin cannot be retracted, so the sac cannot be cleaned or drained
blocks.caption: Each risk factor either traps moist secretions under the foreskin or weakens host defense against yeast and bacteria.

blocks.text: Diabetes deserves emphasis because it acts twice, as a growth medium and as an immune defect. Recurrent candidal balanitis in an adult man can be the first clue to undiagnosed diabetes mellitus.

Phimosis is a foreskin that cannot be pulled back over the glans. In infants and young boys it is physiologic, because the inner prepuce is still adherent to the glans, and it usually resolves with age. Acquired phimosis results from scarring. Each episode of balanitis heals by fibrosis, which contracts the preputial opening; the tighter opening traps more secretions, which causes further inflammation and more scarring. This self-perpetuating loop explains why recurrent balanitis and phimosis occur together. If a tight foreskin is forced back behind the glans and cannot be returned (paraphimosis), it acts as a constricting band that blocks venous and lymphatic return and causes painful swelling of the glans. Chronic phimosis with retained smegma and inflammation is also a recognized risk factor for penile squamous cell carcinoma.

blocks.title: Balanitis and phimosis feed each other
steps: Moist preputial sac traps smegma and urine
Candida or bacteria overgrow, more so with glycosuria
Glans and inner foreskin become inflamed
Healing fibrosis narrows the preputial opening
Phimosis traps more secretions, renewing infection
blocks.caption: Scarring from each episode tightens the foreskin, and the tighter foreskin sets up the next episode.

blocks.text: The cervix has two epithelia. The ectocervix is covered by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the vagina, and the endocervical canal is lined by mucus-secreting simple columnar epithelium. They meet at the squamocolumnar junction. In adolescents, in pregnancy, and with estrogen-containing contraceptives, this junction often lies out on the ectocervix (ectropion), exposing more columnar cells. This matters because the two main causes of cervicitis prefer columnar epithelium.

Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium. Its infectious elementary body enters columnar cells and becomes a replicating reticulate body inside a membrane-bound inclusion, and the cell later releases new elementary bodies. Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative diplococcus, attaches to columnar cells by pili and Opa proteins and is carried across the epithelium, where its lipooligosaccharide triggers a strong neutrophil response. Both cause endocervicitis: mucopurulent discharge from the os and a friable cervix that bleeds when touched with a swab, because the inflamed mucosa is edematous and hypervascular. Many infections, especially chlamydial ones, cause no symptoms, so they persist and can ascend silently (C07). Gonococci may be seen on Gram stain as gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils, though this is less sensitive from the cervix than from the male urethra; chlamydia does not appear on Gram stain, and both are detected by nucleic acid amplification testing (NAAT).

Two other organisms inflame the cervix but target squamous epithelium and look different. Trichomonas vaginalis, a flagellated protozoan, damages vaginal and ectocervical cells by direct contact and produces punctate subepithelial hemorrhages, the strawberry cervix, with frothy yellow-green malodorous discharge and vaginal pH above 4.5. Herpes simplex virus (HSV-2, and increasingly HSV-1) lyses the squamous cells it infects, producing vesicles that break down into shallow painful ulcers; on the cervix this gives an ulcerative, sometimes necrotic cervicitis, often with vulvar lesions and tender inguinal nodes in a first episode.

blocks.title: Distinguishing the patterns of cervicitis
rows: NAAT positive; not seen on Gram stain
Motile flagellated trichomonads on wet mount
Multinucleated cells with intranuclear inclusions; PCR positive
blocks.caption: Columnar-cell organisms give mucopurulent endocervicitis; squamous-cell organisms give punctate hemorrhage or ulceration.

sections.title: Endometriosis: origin, cyclic bleeding, and symptoms

blocks.text: Endometriosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus. It affects about 10% of women of reproductive age and a much larger share of women evaluated for infertility or chronic pelvic pain. The ovaries are the most common site, followed by the uterosacral ligaments, rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas), and pelvic peritoneum; less often it involves bowel, bladder, and surgical scars, and rarely distant sites such as lung. A lesion is confirmed histologically by two of three features: endometrial glands, endometrial stroma, and hemosiderin pigment from old bleeding.

blocks.title: Theories of origin
rows: Menstrual tissue flows backward through the tubes and implants on pelvic surfaces
The pelvic and ovarian distribution, concentrated in dependent sites such as the rectouterine pouch
Peritoneal and ovarian surface mesothelium, derived from coelomic epithelium, differentiates into endometrium
Rare disease in people who have not menstruated
Endometrial cells travel through veins or lymphatics, a benign metastasis
Lesions in lymph nodes, lung, and other distant sites
Circulating progenitor cells, possibly from bone marrow, differentiate at ectopic sites
Distant lesions and the variety of sites
blocks.caption: No single theory explains every case; each accounts best for a different distribution of lesions.

blocks.text: Retrograde menstruation is the most widely accepted explanation, but it occurs in most menstruating women, so implantation and survival depend on other factors. Endometriotic tissue differs from normal endometrium: its stromal cells express aromatase and make their own estrogen, they produce large amounts of prostaglandin E2, which stimulates aromatase further, they resist the growth-restraining effect of progesterone, and they recruit inflammatory cells. Defective peritoneal clearance of refluxed cells and genetic susceptibility also contribute.

Implants keep their estrogen and progesterone receptors, so they proliferate and bleed with each cycle, but the blood has no way out. Blood and its breakdown products attract macrophages and provoke inflammation followed by fibrosis. Grossly this produces red-blue to yellow-brown nodules (powder-burn lesions). In the ovary, repeated bleeding into a cyst concentrates old blood into an endometrioma, the chocolate cyst. Fibrosis binds tubes, ovaries, uterus, and bowel together and can fix the uterus in retroversion.

blocks.title: Endometriosis: from implant to symptoms
steps: Endometrial glands and stroma lie on ovary or peritoneum
Implants respond to cyclic estrogen and progesterone and bleed
Trapped blood triggers inflammation and prostaglandin release
Fibrosis forms adhesions; ovarian bleeding forms chocolate cysts
Dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, painful defecation, and infertility follow
blocks.caption: Cyclic bleeding with no outlet converts hormone-responsive implants into inflammation and scar.

blocks.text: Each symptom follows from where the inflammation and scarring sit. Dysmenorrhea comes from cyclic bleeding and high local prostaglandin levels; it often begins before menses and is more severe than ordinary cramps. Deep dyspareunia comes from stretching inflamed, scarred uterosacral ligaments and rectouterine pouch during intercourse, and painful defecation means rectal or rectovaginal involvement. Infertility results from adhesions that distort the tube and ovary and block ovum pickup, and from inflammatory peritoneal fluid that impairs gametes, fertilization, and implantation. The uterus itself is normal in size. Symptom severity correlates poorly with the amount of disease. Endometriosis also slightly increases the risk of clear cell and endometrioid ovarian carcinoma.

blocks.predict: What would happen to endometriotic implants and pelvic pain if ovarian estrogen production stopped, as after menopause?
blocks.explain: Implants depend on estrogen to proliferate and bleed, so they usually regress and cyclic pain lessens, but existing adhesions and fibrosis persist because scar tissue does not depend on hormones.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraphs on hormone receptors in implants and on local aromatase.

sections.title: Adenomyosis compared with endometriosis and leiomyoma

blocks.text: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, separated from the overlying endometrium by normal muscle. It is usually defined as endometrial tissue more than about 2 to 2.5 mm below the endometrial-myometrial junction. The foci arise from the basal layer (stratum basalis), which grows down into the muscle, and the surrounding smooth muscle undergoes reactive hypertrophy. The result is a globular, uniformly enlarged uterus with a thickened wall, rarely larger than about a 12-week pregnancy. It is most common in parous women in their 40s, and prior uterine surgery such as cesarean delivery or curettage is a risk factor, consistent with disruption of the boundary between endometrium and muscle.

Heavy menstrual bleeding is explained by an enlarged endometrial surface and by infiltrated myometrium that contracts poorly, since myometrial contraction helps limit menstrual blood loss. Dysmenorrhea comes from prostaglandin release and from swelling and bleeding of foci inside the muscle. Because basalis-derived glands respond less fully to the cycle, the amount of bleeding within foci varies. On examination the uterus is symmetrically enlarged, soft or boggy, and tender, especially around menses.

Leiomyomas (fibroids) are the most common uterine tumor. They are benign, estrogen-sensitive, clonal proliferations of smooth muscle, often carrying MED12 mutations, and they form discrete, well-circumscribed nodules that push the surrounding muscle aside. That is why they make the uterus irregular and lumpy rather than evenly enlarged. Location predicts symptoms: submucosal tumors distort the cavity and cause heavy bleeding and infertility, while intramural and subserosal tumors press on bladder or rectum. All three conditions are estrogen dependent and often coexist in the same patient.

blocks.title: Endometriosis, adenomyosis, and leiomyoma
rows: Glands and stroma outside the uterus
Glands and stroma within the myometrium
Normal size; may be fixed and retroverted
Heavy bleeding, mainly with submucosal tumors
Powder-burn implants, chocolate cysts; glands, stroma, hemosiderin
Ill-defined foci deep in hypertrophied muscle; no capsule
Sharply circumscribed whorled gray-white nodules of bland smooth muscle
Reproductive age; more common in Black women
blocks.caption: The size and shape of the uterus on examination usually separates the three.

blocks.title: Reading the uterus on examination
blocks.text: A 44-year-old woman with three children has increasingly heavy, painful periods. Step 1: heavy bleeding plus dysmenorrhea narrows the choice to adenomyosis or leiomyoma, since endometriosis does not usually increase menstrual blood loss. Step 2: examine the uterus. A symmetrically enlarged, soft, tender uterus means diffuse infiltration of the wall with reactive hypertrophy, which is adenomyosis. A firm, irregular, lumpy uterus means discrete expanding nodules, which is leiomyoma. Step 3: if instead the uterus were normal in size but fixed, with deep dyspareunia and tender nodularity behind the cervix, the disease would lie outside the uterus, which is endometriosis. Her age and parity also fit adenomyosis.

The closed cervix and its mucus plug normally keep vaginal flora out of the endometrial cavity. Endometritis develops when that barrier is breached and the cavity contains material that supports bacterial growth. Acute and chronic forms are separated by the clinical setting and by the inflammatory cells in the tissue.

Acute endometritis is most often postpartum. After delivery the placental site is a large raw wound, the decidua is partly necrotic, and blood and lochia fill the cavity, an excellent culture medium. Cesarean delivery is the strongest risk factor; prolonged labor or rupture of membranes, repeated vaginal examinations, chorioamnionitis, manual removal of the placenta, and retained placental fragments add to the risk. Miscarriage or abortion with retained products creates the same setting. The infection is polymicrobial from the lower genital tract: streptococci (including group B), gram-negative rods such as E. coli, Gardnerella, and anaerobes such as Bacteroides and Peptostreptococcus. Group A streptococcus causes rare but rapidly severe puerperal sepsis.

The patient has fever of 38.0°C (100.4°F) or more in the days after delivery, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia from anaerobic metabolism. Leukocytosis helps less than usual, because the white cell count normally rises after delivery. Untreated infection extends to the parametrium, pelvic veins (septic pelvic thrombophlebitis), peritoneum, and bloodstream. Histologically, neutrophils infiltrate the endometrium.

Chronic endometritis is persistent low-grade inflammation, often with few symptoms. It is associated with retained products of conception, an intrauterine device, PID (especially chlamydial), and, where it is endemic, tuberculosis, which produces granulomas. Lymphocytes and small lymphoid aggregates are normal in endometrium, and neutrophils are normal during menstruation, so neither proves endometritis. Plasma cells are not normally present; finding them in the stroma, confirmed if needed with CD138 (syndecan-1) staining, marks sustained antigen stimulation and is the diagnostic feature. The inflamed lining sheds and repairs irregularly and is less receptive to an embryo, which explains abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain, infertility, and recurrent pregnancy loss.

blocks.title: Acute versus chronic endometritis
rows: After delivery (especially cesarean), miscarriage, or abortion; retained products
Retained products, intrauterine device, PID, tuberculosis
Polymicrobial genital flora with anaerobes; group A streptococcus rarely
Chlamydia, mixed flora, M. tuberculosis; often none identified
Plasma cells in the endometrial stroma
Parametritis, pelvic abscess, septic thrombophlebitis, sepsis
blocks.caption: Neutrophils with fever after delivery mean acute endometritis; plasma cells in the stroma mean chronic endometritis.

blocks.text: Orchitis is inflammation of the testis. Isolated orchitis is uncommon; most cases are either viral orchitis from mumps or bacterial infection that spreads from the epididymis. The two differ in route, patient age, and consequence.

Mumps virus, a paramyxovirus, spreads by respiratory droplets, replicates in the upper airway and regional lymph nodes, and reaches glandular organs by viremia. Orchitis develops in roughly a fifth to a third of males who get mumps after puberty, usually about 4 to 8 days after parotitis begins, and is rare before puberty. It is unilateral in most cases. The testis becomes painful and swollen, often with high fever. The lesion is an interstitial orchitis with edema and lymphocytic infiltration. Because the tunica albuginea is a tough, nondistensible capsule, edema raises the pressure inside the testis, compresses the seminiferous tubules, and causes ischemic loss of germinal epithelium. Testicular atrophy follows in a substantial share of affected testes, with reduced sperm counts; complete sterility is uncommon because involvement is usually one-sided. Leydig cells are relatively spared, so testosterone is usually preserved.

Bacterial epididymo-orchitis begins in the epididymis. Organisms ascend backward from the urethra or infected urine along the vas deferens to the tail of the epididymis, then spread to the testis. Age and sexual history predict the organism. In sexually active men under about 35 years, C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae from urethritis predominate, often with dysuria or urethral discharge. In older men, E. coli and other enteric gram-negative rods predominate, reflecting urinary infection from prostatic enlargement, obstruction, or catheterization; enteric organisms also occur in men who have insertive anal intercourse.

Pain and swelling develop over hours to days, beginning at the posterior epididymis. The cremasteric reflex is preserved and Doppler ultrasound shows increased blood flow from inflammatory hyperemia. Testicular torsion, the key alternative, begins suddenly, abolishes the cremasteric reflex, and shows absent flow. Bacterial infection can cause abscess, testicular infarction from venous compression, and scarring of the epididymal duct, which causes obstructive infertility when bilateral.

blocks.title: Mumps orchitis and bacterial epididymo-orchitis
rows: Older men; urinary obstruction or instrumentation
E. coli and other gram-negative rods
blocks.caption: Bloodstream spread to the testis means mumps; backward spread along the vas means bacterial epididymo-orchitis, with the organism set by age and sexual history.

sections.title: Pelvic inflammatory disease as ascending infection

blocks.text: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is infection of the upper female genital tract: endometrium, fallopian tubes, ovaries, and pelvic peritoneum, alone or together. It begins as an endocervical infection that ascends. C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae start many cases, but the upper tract infection is usually polymicrobial and includes vaginal flora, especially the anaerobes and Gardnerella of bacterial vaginosis, along with Haemophilus influenzae, enteric gram-negative rods, streptococci, and Mycoplasma genitalium. In a substantial share of cases neither gonorrhea nor chlamydia is found.

The closed cervix and its mucus plug normally limit ascent. Menses weakens this barrier: the os opens slightly, protective mucus is replaced by blood, which is a good culture medium, and retrograde menstrual flow can carry organisms upward. This is why gonococcal PID often begins within a week after a period. Other risks are young age, new or multiple partners, prior PID or STI, bacterial vaginosis, and instrumentation, including intrauterine device insertion, with risk concentrated in the first few weeks after insertion.

blocks.title: Ascending path of PID
steps: C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae infects endocervical columnar cells
Menses opens the barrier; vaginal flora join the infection
Pus spills from the fimbriae into the pelvic peritoneum
Healing fibrosis scars tubes and forms adhesions
blocks.caption: Each step up the tract adds an organ, a symptom, and a site of later scarring.

blocks.text: The organisms injure the tube differently. Gonococci attach to nonciliated mucosal cells, and their lipooligosaccharide and peptidoglycan fragments kill neighboring ciliated cells, producing acute suppurative salpingitis with marked pain. Chlamydia often causes mild or no symptoms, yet tubal damage is substantial because persistent or repeated infection drives a cell-mediated immune response, in part directed at chlamydial heat shock protein 60, that scars the mucosa.

The examination findings map onto the inflamed organs. Moving the cervix pulls on inflamed tubes and parametrium, producing cervical motion tenderness; pressing on the adnexa compresses swollen tubes and ovaries, producing adnexal tenderness; uterine tenderness reflects endometritis; and lower abdominal pain reflects peritoneal inflammation. Fever above about 38.3°C (101°F), purulent cervical discharge, many neutrophils on vaginal wet mount, and raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate or C-reactive protein indicate active inflammation. Ectopic pregnancy produces similar pain, so pregnancy must be excluded with a human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) test.

blocks.predict: Why does chlamydial PID cause as much tubal infertility as gonococcal PID, even though it often causes few symptoms?
blocks.explain: Chlamydial damage comes largely from the host's cell-mediated immune response to persistent or repeated infection, which scars the tubal mucosa without much pain, and because symptoms are mild the infection continues longer before it is recognized.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on how gonococci and chlamydia injure the tube.

blocks.text: Salpingitis, inflammation of the fallopian tube, is the central lesion of PID. Its complications follow from three facts. The tubal mucosa is a delicate, folded (plicae), ciliated epithelium that must move an ovum and embryo toward the uterus. The fimbriated end opens into the peritoneal cavity. And inflammation in every one of these sites heals by fibrosis.

blocks.title: Complications of salpingitis and their mechanisms
rows: Pus accumulates in a tube whose fimbriated end has closed
Fimbrial end stays sealed; pus resorbs and the tube fills with watery secretion
Inflamed tube adheres to the ovary and a polymicrobial, anaerobe-rich abscess forms
Adnexal mass and fever; rupture causes peritonitis and sepsis
Cilia destroyed, plicae fused, fimbriae occluded, peritubal adhesions
Risk rises with each episode of PID
Damaged but open tube passes sperm yet delays the embryo
Tubal implantation, usually in the ampulla; rupture with hemorrhage
Infected exudate reaches the liver capsule
Right upper quadrant pain; violin-string adhesions
blocks.caption: Closure of the fimbriated end, loss of cilia, and fibrosis account for nearly every complication.

blocks.text: Ectopic pregnancy shows how partial damage can be more dangerous than complete obstruction. A completely blocked tube prevents pregnancy, but a tube whose lumen stays open while its cilia are lost and its folds are bridged by adhesions lets small sperm reach the ovum yet fails to carry the much larger embryo to the uterus. The embryo implants in the tube, most often the ampulla, whose thin wall cannot support it, and rupture causes intraperitoneal bleeding. Prior salpingitis is one of the most important risk factors for ectopic pregnancy.

Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is inflammation of the liver capsule (perihepatitis) that complicates both chlamydial and gonococcal PID. Infected exudate from the open fimbriae is thought to travel up the right paracolic gutter, the main peritoneal channel from the pelvis to the space around the liver, although lymphatic spread has also been proposed. The capsule and adjacent parietal peritoneum are inflamed but the liver parenchyma is not, so liver enzymes are normal or only mildly raised. Sharp right upper quadrant pain worsens with breathing and may be referred to the right shoulder, because diaphragmatic peritoneum is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5). Fibrinous exudate heals into fine violin-string adhesions between the anterior liver surface and the anterior abdominal wall or diaphragm, seen at laparoscopy.

blocks.title: Right upper quadrant pain that is not the gallbladder
blocks.text: A 24-year-old woman has sharp right upper quadrant pain that worsens on deep breathing, fever, and lower abdominal pain. Ultrasound shows a normal gallbladder, and liver enzymes are near normal. Step 1: pleuritic upper abdominal pain with normal parenchymal tests points to inflamed capsule or peritoneum rather than liver cells or gallbladder. Step 2: lower abdominal pain with fever in a young sexually active woman suggests PID; cervical motion and adnexal tenderness on pelvic examination would confirm the source. Step 3: link them. Exudate from inflamed fimbriae tracks up the right paracolic gutter to the liver capsule, which is Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis. Step 4: predict the laparoscopic finding, violin-string adhesions from liver capsule to abdominal wall.

The adult vagina is lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium that stores glycogen under the influence of estrogen. Glycogen from shed cells is broken down to simpler sugars that lactobacilli ferment to lactic acid, holding vaginal pH at about 3.8 to 4.5. Lactobacilli also compete for nutrients and attachment sites. Candida albicans, which causes most cases, lives harmlessly in the vagina of a sizable minority of women, so disease means overgrowth and tissue invasion, not mere presence. Candida tolerates acid and lactobacilli usually persist, so unlike bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis, candidal vaginitis does not raise the pH.

Symptomatic infection follows a switch from budding yeast to invasive hyphae and pseudohyphae that adhere to and penetrate the epithelium. Hyphae secrete aspartyl proteases and the peptide toxin candidalysin, which damage epithelial cells and trigger neutrophil recruitment; much of the itching, burning, and redness is this host inflammatory response. Mucosal defense depends on Th17 cells, through interleukin 17 and interleukin 22, and on neutrophils.

blocks.title: Risk factors for candidal vaginitis
rows: Kill lactobacilli, removing competition for nutrients and attachment sites
High glucose in tissue and secretions feeds yeast; neutrophil function is impaired
Estrogen raises epithelial glycogen and promotes yeast adherence and hyphal growth
Loss of T-cell defense (for example HIV infection or corticosteroids) allows mucosal overgrowth
blocks.caption: Risk factors remove bacterial competition, add fuel for yeast, or weaken T-cell control.

blocks.text: The discharge is thick, white, and curd-like, resembling cottage cheese, with little odor. The vulva is itchy, red, and swollen, sometimes with satellite lesions, and urine on inflamed skin causes burning on urination. The pH is normal (4.5 or less) and the whiff (amine) test is negative. A 10% potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation dissolves epithelial cells but not fungal cell walls, revealing pseudohyphae and budding yeast. Candida glabrata, a less common cause, forms only budding yeast without pseudohyphae.

blocks.title: The three common causes of vaginal discharge
rows: Pseudohyphae and budding yeast on KOH
blocks.caption: A normal pH with itching and curd-like discharge points to Candida; a raised pH points to bacterial vaginosis or trichomoniasis.

blocks.predict: Why does candidal vaginitis leave vaginal pH normal while bacterial vaginosis raises it?
blocks.explain: Candida grows well in acid and lactobacilli usually persist, so lactic acid production continues; in bacterial vaginosis lactobacilli are replaced by anaerobes, lactic acid falls, and amine production raises the pH.
blocks.check: Compare with the first paragraph of this section on glycogen, lactobacilli, and pH.

blocks.text: Lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory skin disease with a strong preference for anogenital skin. It is most common in postmenopausal women, with a smaller peak in prepubertal girls, and it also affects men, where it involves the glans and foreskin and is a cause of acquired phimosis (C01). Its cause is not settled. It is considered immune mediated, it is associated with autoimmune diseases such as autoimmune thyroid disease and vitiligo, and many patients have autoantibodies against extracellular matrix protein 1.

The histology explains the appearance. The epidermis is thinned, with loss of rete ridges and degeneration of basal cells. Beneath it, the upper dermis is replaced by a band of pale, homogeneous, nearly acellular (hyalinized) collagen, and below that band lies a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate. Thin epidermis over pale, poorly vascular collagen looks white and shiny and wrinkles like parchment or cigarette paper. Thin skin tears and bruises easily, so purpura and fissures are common.

Intense itching is the main symptom, and scratching adds further injury. White plaques may encircle the vulva and anus in a figure-of-eight pattern. Progressive sclerosis and contraction distort the anatomy: the labia minora shrink or fuse, the clitoral hood scars over, and the introitus narrows, causing dyspareunia. The vagina, lined by mucosa rather than skin, is typically spared.

Lichen sclerosus carries a small increase in the risk of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, often quoted as a few percent over a lifetime. This pathway does not involve human papillomavirus (HPV). Chronic inflammation and epithelial injury in older women lead to TP53 mutations and differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia, then keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma. HPV-associated vulvar carcinoma, by contrast, arises from high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions in younger women. A persistent ulcer, nodule, or thickened area arising within lichen sclerosus is therefore suspicious for this progression.

blocks.title: White or thinned vulvar skin: three causes
rows: Thin, with loss of rete ridges
Band of hyalinized collagen with lymphocytes beneath
blocks.caption: Lichen sclerosus thins the epidermis and scars the dermis; lichen simplex chronicus thickens the epidermis.

integration.text: Histology and anatomy predict where each organism settles and where harm accumulates. Chlamydia and gonococci seek columnar epithelium in the endocervix, tubes, and male urethra, while Trichomonas, HSV, and Candida infect squamous surfaces of the vagina, ectocervix, and glans. The open fimbriae connect the female tract to the peritoneal cavity, so cervical infection can reach the pelvis and the liver capsule, while in men organisms travel backward along the vas to the epididymis. Mumps is the exception that arrives by blood. In both sexes healing by fibrosis turns inflammation into lasting damage: phimosis, tubal occlusion, ectopic pregnancy, epididymal obstruction, and pelvic adhesions.

Endocrinology and immunology explain the rest. Estrogen maintains vaginal glycogen and acidity and drives growth of ectopic and intramyometrial endometrium, so endometriosis and adenomyosis are diseases of the reproductive years, while T-cell immunity governs Candida and the immune response to Chlamydia causes much of the tubal scarring. Pelvic findings overlap widely among PID, ectopic pregnancy, endometriosis, and appendicitis, so a single sign rarely decides the answer; the setting, timing, and laboratory clues do.

summary: Balanitis comes from Candida or bacteria in a moist preputial sac; uncircumcised foreskin, poor hygiene, and diabetes are risks, and scarring from recurrent episodes causes phimosis, which traps more secretions.
C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae infect endocervical columnar cells and cause mucopurulent cervicitis with a friable cervix; Trichomonas gives a strawberry cervix and HSV an ulcerative cervicitis.

Endometriosis is endometrial glands and stroma outside the uterus; implants bleed cyclically, causing inflammation, adhesions, chocolate cysts, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, and infertility with a normal-sized uterus.
Adenomyosis is endometrium within the myometrium, giving a uniformly enlarged, boggy, tender uterus with heavy painful periods; leiomyoma gives an irregular, firm, nodular uterus.
Acute endometritis is polymicrobial infection after delivery, especially cesarean, or retained products, with fever and uterine tenderness; plasma cells in the stroma define chronic endometritis.
Mumps orchitis is bloodborne, postpubertal, and can cause atrophy; epididymo-orchitis ascends along the vas, from STI organisms in young men and E. coli in older men.
PID is ascending polymicrobial infection started by C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae; cervical motion, adnexal, and uterine tenderness reflect the inflamed organs.

Salpingitis heals by fibrosis, causing hydrosalpinx, tubo-ovarian abscess, tubal infertility, and ectopic pregnancy; spread to the liver capsule causes Fitz-Hugh-Curtis perihepatitis with violin-string adhesions.
Candidal vaginitis follows antibiotics, diabetes, pregnancy, or immunosuppression and gives thick white discharge, itching, normal pH, and pseudohyphae on KOH.
Lichen sclerosus thins the epidermis over hyalinized dermis, forms white parchment-like plaques in older women, and slightly raises the risk of HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma.

verify: Endometriosis prevalence (about 10% of reproductive-age women) and its share among infertile women vary between sources.

The depth threshold for adenomyosis (about 2 to 2.5 mm below the endometrial-myometrial junction) and the typical maximum uterine size differ between sources; sources also disagree on how much adenomyotic foci bleed cyclically, since they derive from the basal layer.
Mumps orchitis figures (incidence after puberty, onset about 4 to 8 days after parotitis, proportion of affected testes that atrophy) vary between series.
The age of about 35 years separating STI-related from enteric epididymitis follows public health guidance; confirm the cutoff NABNE expects.
The proportion of PID in which C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae is identified has fallen in recent series; the fever threshold of about 38.3°C (101°F) comes from clinical diagnostic criteria.
Whether Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is more often chlamydial or gonococcal differs by source; it is stated here as complicating both.

The lifetime vulvar squamous cell carcinoma risk in lichen sclerosus is quoted from about 2% to 5%; the role of antibodies to extracellular matrix protein 1 is supported but not established as causal.
A visible strawberry cervix is seen in only a small minority of trichomoniasis cases without colposcopy; confirm how NABNE frames it.
Adenomyosis and lichen sclerosus are not in the NABNE condition list for this category (they come from the USMLE outline); confirm they are in scope.

Requested new diagram names: pid-ascent (female tract showing the path from cervix to tubes, pelvis, and liver capsule), uterine-lesions (sites of endometriosis, adenomyosis, and leiomyoma), and cervix-epithelia (squamocolumnar junction and ectropion).
